doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Teaching big band and symphony writing; getting music played
summary: Abene describes the Manhattan School of Music course on writing for big band and symphony and the difficulty of hearing your music played; radio and service bands are the closest thing to Ellington's own group.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yes. It’s very interesting because I’m so used to doing two and three hour seminars. And the thing is when you do 50 minutes it’s so — you know you talk about being confined, especially in the subject, in this instance of talking about writing for big band and symphony combined, which is a course that the late Manny Albam and I initiated at Manhattan School of Music and along with the help of Justin DeCioccio, who is the head of the jazz department there. So you’re talking about quite a — it’s not, you’re not talking about all the writing for five horns or writing for big band, it’s so much more involved. And just the questions, trying to answer one of those questions could take five or ten minutes.
Plus isn’t it, it would seem like you’d be getting questions that you can’t really answer until you like work backwards and say first your deal with this before you can even deal with that.

That’s right. And the biggest question you get is, well obviously what you — how do you get your music played, which you know coming from someone like myself who is basically self taught and the way I did it was you know you write and you go out and throw yourself out there and try to hear it played by anybody. You know, who cares, as long as you’re hearing something played. Obviously it’s hard enough to sometimes deal with a trio or a big band, much less now you’re suddenly dealing with an orchestral thing. But a lot of the students, a lot of the people who have access who are in universities who are even teachers or students or who have access to people at universities who can certainly, or music I should say music colleges, there’s no excuse for not really killing yourself and making sure you can get these groups together. Or even write something for string quartet and see how that sounds. Just get the sound of everything in your head. So ©Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
and it’s hard to answer those questions. It’s like how am I going to become original? Oh okay, here’s what you do, it’s how you become an original.
The days of people like Ellington having their own group to hear things immediately —

That’s gone, I mean that’s gone. And the closest thing you have today, are the radio bands in Europe, mostly in Europe. And what you have in the United States the closest thing to that is the armed service bands and orchestras where you have — people are hired for X amount of weeks a year, you don’t send in a sub you know. And certainly not in the armed service bands, but even the radio bands. You have to have, those people you send in for a sub if you’re on a vacation or something, they have to be approved. So you can’t just send, it’s not like well it’s a pick-up band. So you have the advantage of working with a band that is there 50 weeks a year, 48 weeks a year. So it really helps when you try to listen to your music, and that’s for sure.
